### PROCESS LXXVII.
**Tincture of Tartarized Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**ake Tartarized Tartar, duly prepared according to Process 75, and dried, then ground into a fine powder. Pour over it, in a tall chemical vial, the purest Alcohol of wine to a depth of four inches. Then, with the vial closed only with paper, let them boil together, as gently as possible, in our wooden furnace for the space of twenty-four hours. The Alcohol will be of a golden color, floating on top, with an aromatic odor and a penetrating, warm taste. If this is repeated with fresh Alcohol in the same manner, a white salt will eventually be left at the bottom. The tinctures are thickened by a gentle fire, so that a tenth part remains, concentrated at the bottom.

#### USES.
**I**t serves to demonstrate the part in that Salt which is dissolved by the Alcohol. The Tincture itself, when prepared, is aromatic and warming, and consolidates ulcers and wounds. The remaining salt, being simpler than before, teaches that salts themselves can be whitened, once the tincture has been drawn out by the aid of Alcohol.

### PROCESS LXXVIII.
**Dissolution of Regenerated Tartar in Alcohol.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**ake Regenerated Tartar, prepared as neatly as possible beforehand, and, as safely as can be done, pour six times its amount of the purest Alcohol into a tall, glass chemical vial. Boil it over a gentle fire in our wooden furnace, as prudently as possible. They will combine with each other, and these will become one uniformly composed substance, with the dregs deposited at the bottom. After they have then settled accurately through rest, let the supernatant and pure liquor flow off by a careful tilting of the vessel. If any saline matter not yet dissolved remains, it can be dissolved by the application of fresh Alcohol with the same caution, and separated from the dregs. Then indeed, let the prepared liquors be thickened by distilling over a very gentle fire until they are reduced to half, and the Tincture of this Salt will be obtained.

#### USES.
**Y**ou see in this experiment united into one: alkali, oily acid, and the oil of spirits of vegetables. Hence, the most active principles of plants are freed from inert earth; yet at the same time they are sufficiently safe, and their acrimony is no longer dangerous. These, indeed, when thus united, seem to constitute even the small Elixir of the Sages, which the masters of the ancient Art recommended for preserving and restoring health. It heals almost all obstructions, penetrates through the vessels, <column-break/>
and excites life with an agreeable stimulus: it heals through perspiration. In chemical operations, it also provides a most effective solvent, by which substances are reduced to their smallest parts, with their active, seminal virtue unimpaired, so that they may be admitted into the inner chambers of the body to check and tame whatever is rebellious. Nor is this remedy less praised for the beauty of the effects it produces on external bodily ailments, wounds, ulcers, and tumors. Yet this remedy, being so wholesome, should not be denied to the poor out of ambition: for it can be prepared immediately by mixing potash <note>original: "Cineres clavellatos"</note> with fifteen parts of the sharpest Vinegar, filtering, and thickening it. Thus, it can be prepared and used without the expense of labor and cost. Known to the ancients in Rome. Pliny, Book XXIII, in the Preface: "The ash of vine-shoots, sprinkled with vinegar, is drunk for ailments of the spleen."

### PROCESS LXXIX.
**Harvey’s Tincture of Salt of Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
**I** take the alkaline salt, very black, which remained in the glass retort after all the volatile matter had been expelled by the highest sand heat in the distillation from Tartar, according to (Process 55). To this, quickly pounded into a powder in a hot iron mortar by a hot pestle, and placed into a tall glass vial, I pour the best common spirits of wine, such that they stand four fingers above it. I boil it over a gentle fire in this tall vial, in our wooden furnace, for twenty hours. A black, thin liquor will be obtained, with a bitter, aromatic, and lixivial taste. Let this be poured off pure. Thus, it may be kept safely in a closed vessel for its due uses, under its own title.

#### USES.
**C**ommon Spirit of Wine, consisting of water, acid, and alcohol united, when boiled with the alkali of Tartar—which is still oily—makes a lixivium that is milder and safer because the alkali is tempered by the acid, oil, and alcohol. From this, a species of medicine and solvent is born that is not ignoble. When this is cooked or digested in Chemistry with vegetables, it works well by beautifully dissolving the simples. In surgery, it is a most noble remedy for purifying, cleansing, drying, and consolidating moist, purulent, putrid, sanious, virulent, and cacoethic ulcers, as well as those that are fistulous, sinuous, and consuming the parts with channels. It is also used to consume growths that arise from excessive flesh, especially if it is mixed with a little oil according to art.
